```{r}
source("R/helpers.R")
set.seed(STUDENT_SEED)

binomial_size <- 5
probability <- 0.10
population_mean <- binomial_size * probability
population_sd <- sqrt(binomial_size * probability * (1 - probability))
generator <- function(sample_size) {
  rbinom(sample_size, size = binomial_size, prob = probability)
}
```

## Question and prediction

This population is discrete and strongly concentrated near zero because the
probability of success is only 0.10. I expect it to need a larger sample size
than a symmetric population before its sample means look smooth and normal.

The theoretical mean is `r population_mean` and the theoretical standard
deviation is `r round(population_sd, 4)`.

## Original population

```{r}
population <- rbinom(10000, size = binomial_size, prob = probability)
plot_population_bar(
  population,
  "Original Small Binomial population",
  "Number of successes"
)
```

The original distribution is discrete and right-skewed. This makes it a useful
case for comparing the CLT with the already-symmetric Standard Normal case.

## Simulation and theoretical comparison

```{r}
means_by_size <- simulate_sample_means(generator)
summary_table <- summarize_sample_means(
  means_by_size,
  theoretical_mean = population_mean,
  theoretical_sd = population_sd
)
print_summary(summary_table)
first_screened_n <- summary_table$sample_size[summary_table$screening_rule][1]
chosen_row <- summary_table[summary_table$sample_size == first_screened_n, , drop = FALSE]
```

## Sample sizes investigated

I investigated sample sizes `n = 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, and 200`. I started
with small values to show the discreteness and right skew, included `n = 30`
because it is a common classroom rule, and used larger values to see how many
observations were needed for the sample means to become smoother.

The theoretical standard error is `population_sd / sqrt(n)`. I check whether
the simulated standard deviation approaches that value as `n` increases.

## Visual evidence

```{r}
selected_sizes <- c(5, 20, 50, 100)
plot_selected_diagnostics(means_by_size, selected_sizes, "Small Binomial")
plot_selected_qq(means_by_size, selected_sizes, "Small Binomial Q-Q plot")
```

At small sample sizes, the means can remain visibly discrete. With larger
sample sizes, the spacing between possible means becomes smaller relative to
the overall spread, so the sampling distribution can look more continuous.

## Approximate normal decision

My final answer is **n =** `r first_screened_n`. At this sample size, the
histogram looked smoother and more balanced, and the Q-Q plot was more nearly
straight than it was for the smaller sample sizes. The skewness was
`r round(chosen_row$skewness, 3)`, the excess kurtosis was
`r round(chosen_row$excess_kurtosis, 3)`, and the simulated standard deviation
was `r round(chosen_row$simulated_sd, 4)` compared with a theoretical standard
error of `r round(chosen_row$theoretical_se, 4)`.

The original population is concentrated near zero and is right-skewed. The
sample means become smoother as `n` increases. This value was larger than the
die result, which shows that both skewness and discreteness can slow down the
normal-looking shape.

## What surprised me

I was surprised that the Small Binomial distribution needed a larger sample
size than the die. Even though both populations are discrete, the low success
probability made this population more concentrated and more right-skewed.
